title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
text:
The data comes from Banking Dataset - Marketing Targets. This is picked up from publicly available research data UCI Machine Learning using random sampling plus a few additional columns are introduced in Kaggle data.
In Project 2, I explored this data with an interactive Shiny app. The goal of this (final) project is to predict y y is a categorical outcome of the campaign, therefore we will be working on a binary classification problem.
Client Traits (column names in the data set):



age (numeric)
job : type of job (categorical: “admin.”,“unknown”,“unemployed”,“management”,“housemaid”,“entrepreneur”,“student”,“blue-collar”,“self-employed”,“retired”,“technician”,“services”)
marital : marital status (categorical: “married”,“divorced”,“single”; note: “divorced” means divorced or widowed)
education (categorical: “unknown”,“secondary”,“primary”,“tertiary”)
default: has credit in default? (binary: “yes”,“no”)
balance: average yearly balance, in euros (numeric)
housing: has housing loan? (binary: “yes”,“no”)
loan: has personal loan? (binary: “yes”,“no”)





contact: contact communication type (categorical: “unknown”,“telephone”,“cellular”)
day: last contact day of the month (numeric)
month: last contact month of year (categorical: “jan”, “feb”, “mar”, …, “nov”, “dec”)
duration: last contact duration, in seconds (numeric)





campaign: number of contacts performed during this campaign and for this client (numeric, includes last contact)
pdays: number of days that passed by after the client was last contacted from a previous campaign (numeric, -1. means client was not previously contacted)
previous: number of contacts performed before this campaign and for this client (numeric)
poutcome: outcome of the previous marketing campaign (categorical: “unknown”,“other”,“failure”,“success”)

Output variable (desired target):

y - has the client subscribed a term deposit? (binary: “yes”,“no”)

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
text:
Train/ test split
Let’s select the 5 predictor columns + response column and then do a 70-30 split on the data. Let’s use response as strata so both train and test have same proportion of yes/no observations

set.seed(558)

bank <- bank_all |>
  select(y, housing, poutcome, age, balance, campaign)

bank_split <- initial_split(bank, prop = 0.7, strata = y)
bank_train <- training(bank_split)
bank_test <- testing(bank_split)

Let’s check yes/no balance in both training and testing sets

bank_train |> 
  count(y) |> 
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
text:
Cross validation folds
Using 5 fold cross validation to select best model from each family of models: - classification tree (not regression tree because the response is a categorical/class variable) - random forest

bank_folds <- vfold_cv(bank_train, v = 5, strata = y)
bank_folds

#  5-fold cross-validation using stratification 
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  splits               id   
  <list>               <chr>
1 <split [25317/6330]> Fold1
2 <split [25317/6330]> Fold2
3 <split [25318/6329]> Fold3
4 <split [25318/6329]> Fold4
5 <split [25318/6329]> Fold5


There are 31,647 observations in the training data. 5 fold CV splits them into 5 folds of about 6,330 observations each (or 6329 in some folds). In each of the 5 iterations, the model is fit on 4 folds (about 25,300 observations) and evaluated on the remaining fold which is the validation fold. Each fold serves as the validation fold exactly once. The log-loss is averaged for these 5 iterations.
CV helps to select the hyperparameters that are not influenced by specific subset of training data. Instead all of the training data is used for both fitting and evaluatiing the model in different iterations and for each combination of the tuning-grid/hyperparameter selection
The test set is not used in CV process.

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
section: Metric for selecting the best model from each family
text:
Metric for selecting the best model from each family
I will go with log-loss function. Basically in a classification problem we have to maximize the likelihood of correctly estimating the outcome which translates to minimizing negative likelihood function aka log-loss function. One other option considered is accuracy - however the share of subscribers is about 12%. Therefore, a model that learns to classify every customer as “no” gets it right 88% of the times which is not meaningful. An 88% accuracy would only be meaningful if the outcome classes were balanced.

bank_metrics <- metric_set(mn_log_loss)

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
section: How does the model make predictions?
text:
How does the model make predictions?
In a regression tree, as we saw in HW10, the prediction is the mean of a response variable in a given region. In a classification tree, however, the prediction is the most prevalent class in that region.
Since we are using log-loss as our metric, we are interested in the probability of a client subscribing to a term deposit. This probability can be obtained by looking at the proportion of clients who subscribed within a given terminal node.

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
text:
How does the tree fit?
The fitting is done by recursive binary splitting, which is greedy; it picks the best split that minimizes loss at each step without looking ahead. At each step it tries every predictor and every possible cut point, and chooses the split that makes the two new regions as close to all yes or all no as possible, then repeats this within each new region.

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
text:
What is Pruning?
If we keep splitting, the tree will grow very large and overfit the training data. Trees are usually grown large first and then pruned back using cost-complexity pruning which is controlled by the cost_complexity tuning parameter.

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
section: What are the other tuning parameters?
text:
What are the other tuning parameters?
The other tuning parameter I use this tree_depth, which sets the maximum depth of the tree. The final tree is limited by the stricter of cost_complexity or tree_depth Another parameter, min_n, is the minimum number of observations a node needs before it can split. I will leave it as the default of 20.
I tune cost_complexity and tree_depth together using a grid of 5 values each, which gives 25 combinations. Each combination is fit using the 5-fold CV described above, and the one with the lowest average log-loss is selected

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
text:
Fitting the classificaiton tree

tree_spec <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = tune(), tree_depth = tune()) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")


tree_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(bank_recipe) |>
  add_model(tree_spec)


tree_grid <- grid_regular(cost_complexity(), tree_depth(), levels = 5)

tree_results <- tree_workflow |>
  tune_grid(resamples = bank_folds, grid = tree_grid, metrics = bank_metrics)

# arrange the 25 trees by the mean value of mn_log_loss in ascending order 
collect_metrics(tree_results) |>
  arrange(mean)

The tree splits on poutcome first. if the previous campaign was a success, about 65% of those clients subscribed, but the remaining 97% of clients all go into on leaf with only about 10% chance of subscribing. Interestingly, age is not usued anywhere in the tree even though it looked useful during the EDA.

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
section: How is it different from a single tree?
text:
How is it different from a single tree?
The main difference is that a random forest doesn’t use all the predictors at each split. Instead it picks a random subset of predictors every time it splits, and then the number of predictors it picks is the tuning parameter mtry.
The reason for this is that if there is one really strong predictor, every tree would use it for the first split and all the trees would end up looking very similar. In our classification tree poutcome was the first split. If every tree in the forest also split on poutcome first, the trees would all look about the same, and averaging nearly identical tree wouldn’t yield different results than single tree. By allowing a random subset of predictors at each split, some trees can’t use poutcome at the top, so the trees end up different from each other, and averaging them gives more stable predictions.

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
text:
Why it should do better?
In our classification tree, some of the leaves had ~0% of the clients, so a different training sample might not make those splits at all. Averaging many trees smooths this out and usually gives a better predictions.
The downside of this is we lose interpretability. With many trees (forest) there is no single tree that we can plot and read like above.

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
text:
Tuning?
mtry controls how different trees are from each other. A small mtry means each split only sees a few predictors, so the trees are very different, but some trees may miss strong predictors like poutcome. A large value of mtry makes each tree stronger, but the trees look more alike. when mtry is 5, all splits will use all 5 predictors.
I will tune mtry from 1 to 5 using same CV folds and log-loss as the classification tree. I will pick mtry that has the lowest value of average log-loss function. Then mtry is fixed for the final forest which then every split considers the same number of predictors (but predictors can be different)

title: Bank Marketing: Model Fitting and Selection
text:
Fitting random forest

rf_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = tune()) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("classification")


rf_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(bank_recipe) |>
  add_model(rf_spec)


rf_grid <- grid_regular(mtry(range = c(1,5)), levels = 5)

set.seed(558)

rf_results <- rf_workflow |>
  tune_grid(resamples = bank_folds, grid = rf_grid, metrics = bank_metrics)

# arrange the 5 random forests by the mean value of mn_log_loss in ascending order 
collect_metrics(rf_results) |>
  arrange(mean)
